title: Secondary maths teachers, how well do you know the primary maths curriculum?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton argues that secondary maths teachers often pitch lessons too low because they do not know what students have already met in primary school. He opens with a Year 7 lesson on ordering two-digit numbers, a skill the teacher placed in Year 5 but which England's primary programmes of study introduce in Year 2. Exposure is not mastery, he concedes, but teachers who know the primary curriculum can assess prior knowledge and skip ahead where students are secure. He admits he once treated Year 7s as blank canvases himself. He closes by inviting readers to test their knowledge of which year group each primary objective belongs to.
points: Secondary teachers frequently misjudge when students first met a concept, leading to Key Stage 3 lessons pitched at Key Stage 2 level.
Exposure to an idea is not mastery, so the answer is to assess prior knowledge and respond, not to assume either way.
Studying the Primary Programmes of Study is Barton's recommended remedy.
Barton owns the error, having treated Year 7s as blank canvases for years.
quotes: Of course, encountering an idea is not the same as mastering that idea. However, as secondary school teachers, we need to be aware of the concepts students have been exposed to at primary school - and how many times they have been exposed to them - to shape our teaching better.

He could continue with his planned I Do if the vast majority struggled. However, if most students were secure in this knowledge, he could progress to the next idea, keeping his students challenged and motivated in the process.

This is not an isolated case. I regularly watch Key Stage 3 maths lessons that would not be out of place in Key Stage 2. Time and time again, in the discussion that follows the lesson, the reason the lesson has been pitched as it has is that the secondary school teacher is unaware of their students’ experience at primary school.

Before I came across as too high and mighty, I was in the same boat for many years. I treated my Year 7s as blank canvasses who had perhaps dabbled in addition, subtraction, and the odd times table, so I taught everything else as if it was brand new to them.
See how you get on. If any answer surprises you, think carefully about the implications of how you approach these topics with your students and your Key Stage 3 schemes of work.
